**Databases and data structures** — how stored data is organized so that it can be found and kept current — physical database design and index selection, materialized views and the choice of which answers to precompute, adaptive and self-organizing structures, lower bounds on lookup, caching and paging; and the cost of organizing ahead of use against organizing in use. Read for itself, not as ML practice: learned indexes and other machine-learning approaches go to the anthology (ADR-045).

| [CLAIM-306](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-306.md) | Under a deadline, search can establish presence by finding one item but absence only by exhausting the collection, so "If I can't find it, it isn't there" acts on an unfinished search as negation as failure acts on a finished one: a default stronger than either the closed-world assumption or negation as failure, safe only when the arrangement makes the full search finish within the deadline | The medic's "If I can't find it, it isn't there" ([CASE-085](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-085.md)) and the owner's "if I can't find it quickly enough, it may as well not be there" ([CASE-094](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-094.md)) act on a failed search as if it showed absence. One find shows presence, but absence needs a check of everything, which a deadline forbids. First filed as negation as failure on a time bound, with Reiter and Clark unread. Both readings corrected it. The two assumptions are separate. Reiter's closed-world assumption is that the database is complete about the world. Clark's negation as failure is licensed only by finite failure: "the exhaustive but unsuccessful search for a proof". A search cut off by a deadline meets neither, so the rule is stronger than both. It assumes a closed world and that the unsearched part would have failed. It is safe when the full pass finishes in time. In [CASE-085](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-085.md) the EMT knew the drug was stocked, which is exactly where Reiter shows the closed-world assumption inconsistent. So there it was a decision to stop, not an inference. | Superseded — by [CLAIM-312](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-312.md) |
| [CLAIM-311](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-311.md) | A search cut off before an exhaustive pass can establish absence when the arrangement certifies that the unsearched remainder cannot hold the item: a sorted table answers non-membership in a logarithmic number of probes, and the Threshold Algorithm stops early with its answer proved, so absence needs a certificate about the remainder, not exhaustion; similarity search in high dimension is where no such certificate exists | Filed at the owner's request, from the database readings set against [CLAIM-306](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-306.md)'s asymmetry: presence by one find, absence "only by exhausting the collection". | [CLAIM-312](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-312.md) | "If I can't find it, it isn't there" asserts operational unavailability, that the item will not be put to use before the deadline, not absence: a search that fails by the deadline establishes unavailability outright, and licenses absence only with a certificate that the unsearched remainder cannot hold the item, from exhaustion, from an invariant of the arrangement, or from a closed-world default | Restates [CLAIM-306](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-306.md) at the owner's request, after [CLAIM-311](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-311.md) showed that absence can be established without exhausting a collection. Read so, the rule reports an outcome and needs no default. | [CLAIM-313](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-313.md) v2 | A fixed number of bins realizes one partition only when each item is stored once: with copies, overlapping partitions coexist, as hashing-based similarity search stores each item in many partitions and pays for it in space, so sortings conflict as arrangements only under a one-copy constraint, which binds bricks but not index entries | Filed at the owner's request, from the readings on locality-sensitive hashing (Indyk and Motwani 1998; Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten 2017) set against [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md)'s premise that "a set of k bins realizes one partition of the collection at a time". That holds when each item is in one place. An index can hold many copies, and hashing-based similarity indexes do exactly that, trading the space of the copies against query time on an exact curve. It narrows [CLAIM-310](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-310.md) to collections whose items cannot be copied, which includes the LEGO case; it does not touch the claim about descriptions. | Active |
| [CLAIM-314](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-314.md) | Reusing a filed argument has a recognition cost that a fixed per-use price leaves out: certifying that stored answers cover a new question is NP-complete even for conjunctive queries, grows with the number and size of the stored definitions rather than being a constant per item, and is undefined for an item filed without a statement of what it answers, so each filing raises the cost of later reuse and per-item break-even decisions are not independent | Filed at the owner's request, from the readings on answering queries using views (Levy, Mendelzon, Sagiv and Srivastava 1995; Chandra and Merlin 1977; Halevy 2001). It undermines the premise [CLAIM-308](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-308.md) states, not its arithmetic. The hardness is worst case and over short definitions, partial reuse is cheap, and nothing here is measured on the record. | Proposed |
